sections.heading: Choosing a border and wording
paragraphs: Four border styles let you match the mood of the award, from a plain frame for a school office to a brighter one for a primary class. Type the wording that fits your records, such as the term or the year, and add the date so the certificate can be filed or framed later. Each name you list gets its own landscape page, so a whole class prints in one go.

sections.heading: Tips for a certificate that feels earned
paragraphs: Check the attendance register before you print and keep the criteria the same for everyone, so the award means something. Print on slightly heavier paper, sign by hand with two signatures, and hand it over in front of the class. For staff, the same page works for a perfect attendance month or year.

sections.heading: Large labels that can be read from a distance
paragraphs: Each sheet carries 16 big labels, so the text is easy to read on a high shelf or across a cupboard. Edit the list before printing: one line per label, such as Tax 2025, Warranty cards or Winter clothes. Names you type stay in the page until you change them.

sections.heading: Making the system last
paragraphs: Group things before you label them: decide the categories first, then print one label per group. Use sticky paper for boxes and plain paper with tape or a label holder for files you may rename. Print one sheet for each room and keep the spare labels so new boxes match the old ones.

sections.heading: A name and a table on every card
paragraphs: Each place card has a large name and a smaller line for the table, so guests find their seat without asking. Eight cards fit on a sheet, and you can type the names in the order you want them printed.

sections.heading: Printing and folding
paragraphs: Print on thicker paper or card, cut along the lines and fold so the card stands on the table. Keep the names short and spelled the way guests prefer. Do a test print of one sheet first, and print a few spare cards for last-minute guests. Plan the seating first so the cards come out in a sensible order.

sections.heading: Wording that thanks everyone
paragraphs: A participation certificate says that someone took part, so keep the wording warm and neutral. Type the name, add the event and the date, and choose one of four borders. One landscape page is made for each name, so a whole class, camp or workshop can be printed together.

sections.heading: Printing for a group
paragraphs: Paste or type the list of names, check the spelling once, and print a single test page before the full batch. Use plain paper for a quick handout or heavier paper for a keepsake. Sign each page by hand with the two signature lines so the certificate feels personal.

sections.heading: Ready messages or your own words
paragraphs: Fourteen ready messages cover the common cases, such as Open, Closed, Please knock or Back soon, and you can write your own for anything else. The words are printed in huge letters with a border, so they can be read from a few steps away.

sections.heading: Where signs work best
paragraphs: Print on A4, place the sign at eye level and use tape or a plastic sleeve so it survives a few weeks. For a shop, keep one Open and one Closed sign ready. Add a phone number only if you want people to call, and use clear contrast between the paper and the ink.

sections.heading: Seeing every project at a glance
paragraphs: The tracker has columns for client, project, start, due date, fee, advance and status, so you can see what is running, what is due and what is still unpaid. Fill the sheet on screen before printing, or print it blank and write by hand.

sections.heading: Keeping it useful
paragraphs: Update the status the same day something changes, and write the advance you received so you always know the balance. Start a new sheet each month or quarter to keep it short. It tracks the work, not the tax, so keep your invoices and accounts in the place your accountant expects.

sections.heading: What a good interruption notice says
paragraphs: The notice has a clear heading, the date and time of the interruption, the reason for the work and a line asking residents to store water in advance. People can plan when they know exactly when the water stops and when it should return.

sections.heading: Posting it on time
paragraphs: Put the notice at the entrance, on each lift and on the society board a day or two before the work. Give honest times and update the notice if the work runs late. The same layout works for any planned service interruption if you change the wording. Keep a copy for the society records.

sections.heading: A week laid out by platform
paragraphs: Platforms run down the side and Monday to Sunday across, so one page shows what goes where each day. You can change the platform names to match what you use, such as Instagram, WhatsApp status or YouTube Shorts.

sections.heading: Planning without burning out
paragraphs: Plan the week once, for example on Sunday, and batch the work: write captions together and prepare pictures together. Leave a few empty boxes for news that comes up. Review the page at the end of the week and note what got a reply, so next week's plan is better than this one.

sections.heading: The parts of an office circular
paragraphs: The page has a heading, a reference number, the date, a To line, a subject, the body text and a space for the manager's signature. That is the shape most offices use for a short announcement to staff.

sections.heading: Writing a circular people read
paragraphs: Put the main point in the subject and the first sentence, then add the details in short lines. Use one circular for one topic. Give a date for any action you need, sign it, and keep a copy in the file. If staff must confirm they have read it, add an acknowledgement line in the body.

sections.heading: Small labels for everything that gets lost
paragraphs: Forty-eight small labels fit on one sheet, sized for water bottles, lunch boxes, pencils, notebooks and uniforms. A dashed cut line shows where to cut, and you can print one name or several.

sections.heading: Making labels last
paragraphs: Use sticker or laminate-friendly paper and press the label on a clean, dry surface. For items that are washed often, stick the label inside the lid or on a clothing tag rather than on the outside. Print a second sheet to keep, so you can replace a label that peels off. Check the spelling once before printing.

sections.heading: To, From and a short message
paragraphs: Each gift tag has To, From and Message lines, eight to a sheet, so you can write by hand or type the names first. They suit birthdays, festivals, weddings and thank-you hampers.

sections.heading: Finishing the tags
paragraphs: Print on thicker paper or card, cut them out and punch a hole for a string or ribbon. Write the message in pen so it feels personal. Print one extra sheet for the year, because it is easy to run out at festival time. Tie the tag to the gift or attach it with a small piece of tape.

sections.heading: A polite reminder, not a demand
paragraphs: The notice names the month, says how to pay and ends with a signature block. The wording is meant to be courteous, so it works as a gentle reminder before any stronger step is needed.

sections.heading: Using it fairly
paragraphs: Add the amount or the due date if you want to be specific, and sign it as the person responsible. Do not name individual residents on a public notice. Post it on the notice board or send it in the group, and keep a copy for the records. It is a reminder, not a legal notice, so follow your society's own rules for any further action.

sections.heading: An invitation that gets a response
paragraphs: The notice gives the date, time and place of the celebration and includes a call for volunteers, which is often what makes a society event happen. You can change the festival name and the wording to suit any occasion.

sections.heading: Planning around the notice
paragraphs: Post it two weeks ahead, so people can plan, and again a few days before. Say clearly who to contact to help, and mention contributions only in the way your society agrees. Include a date for the next step if you need to book food or equipment. Keep the tone friendly and short.

sections.heading: Planning posts in advance
paragraphs: The calendar has columns for date, platform, topic, format, caption ready and posted, so you can see the whole plan and what is still unfinished. Format can be a reel, a photo, a story or a short post.

sections.heading: Keeping to the plan
paragraphs: Fill a month at a time and tick Caption ready when the words are done, so it is clear what is waiting for a picture or a video. Tick Posted when it is live. Start with fewer posts than you think you can keep up with, and add more only when the habit is steady. Small shops can plan around festivals and sale dates.

sections.heading: A certificate for a student of the month or year
paragraphs: Type the student's name and choose the wording, the date and one of four borders. It works for best student, student of the month or a similar award, and one landscape page is printed for each name.

sections.heading: Making the award count
paragraphs: Say in the wording what the award is for, such as effort, kindness or improvement, so it does not feel like a prize only for marks. Sign it with both signature lines, print on good paper and hand it over in front of the class. Keep a list of past winners so the choice stays fair over the year.

sections.heading: Labels with Item, Made on and Use by
paragraphs: Each label has three lines: what is inside, the date it was made and the date to use it by. Twenty-four fit on a sheet, so a batch of meal prep can be labelled in one go.

sections.heading: Using the labels safely
paragraphs: Write the Use by date yourself, based on your own guidance and the food, because the page does not tell you how long food keeps. Stick the label on a dry, cool container before it goes in the freezer, and use waterproof ink. You can pre-fill the item names for the dishes you cook every week.

sections.heading: Saying thank you properly
paragraphs: A certificate of appreciation thanks someone for help, service or kindness. Type the name, write a line of thanks, add the date and choose a border. One landscape page is made for each person.

sections.heading: Who it suits
paragraphs: Use it for volunteers, teachers, society helpers, event teams or colleagues who went the extra mile. Make the wording specific, for example what the person did, because a specific thank-you feels sincere. Sign it by hand and hand it over in person. It is a gesture of thanks and not an official document.

sections.heading: Fourteen labels to a sheet
paragraphs: Each label has To: at the top and up to six lines for the address, so you can fit a name, house, street, area, city and phone number. Fourteen labels fit on an A4 sheet.

sections.heading: Printing clearly
paragraphs: Write the address in the order the post office expects, with the PIN code on its own line, and keep the lines short. Use sticker paper and run a test on plain paper first to check the alignment. Small online sellers can print a sheet of labels for the day's orders and stick them on parcels. Do not print the same personal address more often than needed.

sections.heading: Who has which key, and when
paragraphs: The register has columns for date, key or item, taken by, time out, time in and signature. It gives a simple record of who took a key and when it came back.

sections.heading: Keeping the register honest
paragraphs: Keep it at one fixed place and ask everyone to sign out and in. It does not replace a lock, but it makes missing keys easier to trace. It works for lent equipment, shared tools and vehicle keys too. Review the page at the end of each day and make sure every item is back.

sections.heading: Time, topic, leader and minutes
paragraphs: The agenda has columns for time, topic, who leads and how many minutes are allotted, plus meeting and date lines and a notes column. Giving each topic a fixed time keeps the meeting from running over.

sections.heading: Before and during the meeting
paragraphs: Send the agenda in advance so people can prepare. Put decisions first and updates last, and leave a few minutes at the end for anything new. Use the notes column to write what was decided and who does what. The agenda is not the minutes, so keep a separate record of what happened.

sections.heading: Winner, runner-up or participant
paragraphs: Type the name, add the sport and the position, such as first, second or winner, and choose the wording and the border. One landscape page is printed for each name, ready for sports day or a tournament.

sections.heading: Handing out the awards
paragraphs: Check the results sheet before you print so each name and position is right. Print extra pages in case of a mistake. Sign each certificate with the two signature lines and present it at the prize ceremony. Keep the wording the same for each event so the awards look consistent.

sections.heading: Hello, my name is
paragraphs: Each tag has Hello, my name is at the top and a large name below, ten to a sheet. You can type a different name on each tag or print the same name many times.

sections.heading: Using name tags at an event
paragraphs: Print on sticker paper for a classroom, party or workshop, and use plain paper with a clip or pin if stickers are not suitable. Write the names in large letters so they can be read across a table. Print a few spare blanks for late arrivals, and ask guests to wear the tag on the chest.

sections.heading: Recognising good work
paragraphs: The certificate names the employee, includes your wording and the date, and has two signature lines and a border of your choice. Add the month and the company name in the wording to make it specific.

sections.heading: Making recognition fair
paragraphs: Decide the criteria first and share them, such as attendance, customer feedback or teamwork. Print on good paper, sign it by hand and present it at a team meeting. It works for small businesses with a handful of staff as well as larger offices. Keep a note of past winners so the recognition stays fair.

sections.heading: What a gate pass records
paragraphs: Each pass has a number, the date, the name, a phone number, whom to meet, the purpose, the vehicle number, in and out times and signatures. Four passes fit on a page.

sections.heading: Using the passes in a society or office
paragraphs: Add your own society or company name at the top, then cut the pages into slips and keep a copy for the register. It can also be used for material that goes in or out. Give each visitor a number so it is easy to trace later, and keep the used passes for the period your management decides.

sections.heading: Planning tables and seats
paragraphs: You can plan up to 24 tables, six to a page, with a numbered line for each seat. The table names can be edited, so you can call them by family, colour or number.

sections.heading: Making the plan easier
paragraphs: Start with the guest list, group families and friends who should sit together, and then fill the tables. Pencil the names first, because plans change until the last day. Print one copy for the planner and one for the venue. It works for round tables and for long tables.

sections.heading: Name, company, phone and email
paragraphs: The list has columns for name, company, phone, email, last contact and notes, so you can see at a glance who you spoke to and when. It works for clients, customers and vendors.

sections.heading: Keeping contact details safe
paragraphs: A printed list of clients' details should be kept in a safe place and not left open on a desk. Update the last contact column after each call, and use the notes for what was agreed. It is a simple paper list and not a full CRM, but it is easy to start and does not need an account. Shred old pages when you no longer need them.

sections.heading: Wording for a finished course
paragraphs: Type the name, the course and the date, choose one of four borders and print one landscape page for each person. It suits tuition classes, workshops and short courses.

sections.heading: What the certificate is and is not
paragraphs: It is a certificate of completion from you, not an official qualification, so describe the course honestly and sign it by hand. Add the hours or the dates in the wording if you want it to be specific. Print on heavier paper, and keep a list of who received one so you can reissue it if it is lost.

sections.heading: Date, time, place and agenda
paragraphs: The notice gives the date, time and place of the meeting and a list of agenda lines that you can edit. It is suited to societies, clubs and associations.

sections.heading: Giving proper notice
paragraphs: Check your own rules for how much notice you must give and who must receive it, because the page does not set those rules. Post it on the notice board and send it in the group. Keep the agenda short and in the order you will discuss it. Ask members to send their points before the meeting.

sections.heading: Labels for spices, rice, dal and jars
paragraphs: Twenty-four kitchen labels fit on a sheet, with a ready list of common items that you can edit. You can add a small line, such as the date you filled the jar.

sections.heading: Choosing sticker paper
paragraphs: Use water-resistant sticker paper if the jars are near the stove, and press the label on a clean, dry jar. Print one sheet for the whole pantry and keep the spare labels. A clear label helps everyone in the house find things quickly, and makes it easy to see what is running low.

sections.heading: Name, class, subject and school
paragraphs: Each label has lines for name, class, subject and school. You can type the details in or leave them blank to write by hand, and ten labels fit on a sheet.

sections.heading: Labels for the start of the year
paragraphs: Print a sheet per subject, or print blank labels and write the subject in pen. Use sticker paper and place the label on the cover, away from the edges where it can peel. Fill in the child's name once and reuse the same details every year. Keep a spare sheet for new notebooks.

sections.heading: A notice you can adapt
paragraphs: The page has the society name, a date, a subject, the text and a signature. The wording is a starting point that you can change fully to suit the notice.

sections.heading: Writing a clear notice
paragraphs: State the main point in the subject, then add the details in short paragraphs. Include the date, the time and a contact person if residents need to act. Sign it and keep a copy for the records. The wording is general and does not carry any legal force, so follow your society's own rules for formal notices.

sections.heading: Recording complaints and what was done
paragraphs: The register has columns for date, flat, complaint, assigned to, action taken and closed on. It works for societies, offices and shops that want a record of what was reported and how it was handled.

sections.heading: Using it to build trust
paragraphs: Write the complaint the same day, assign a person and fill in the action taken when it is done. Closing the loop is what shows people their complaint was heard. Keep the register private, because it holds names and details, and do not display it on the board. You can also use it as a customer feedback log.

sections.heading: Which invoices are paid
paragraphs: The tracker has columns for invoice number, client, date, amount, due date, paid on and status, so you can see what you have sent and what is still waiting. It tracks invoices and does not create them.

sections.heading: Chasing payments on time
paragraphs: Add each invoice on the day you send it, and look at the due dates every week. Write the paid on date when the money arrives. Status can be sent, overdue or paid. It does not work out tax, so keep your accounts in the way your accountant expects. Start a new page each month for a clear record.

sections.heading: A bubble sheet for practice tests
paragraphs: The sheet has up to 100 questions, with A to D, A to E or true or false choices and optional roll number bubbles. Students fill in a bubble for each answer, which keeps the answers neat and easy to mark.

sections.heading: Marking with a key
paragraphs: Use it for a mock test or a practice paper, and mark with a printed key beside the sheet. It is an OMR-style layout for hand marking, and it is not guaranteed to work with every scanner, so test a sheet before relying on one. Print on plain paper and ask students to fill the bubble fully with a dark pen or pencil.

sections.heading: Who parks where
paragraphs: The register has columns for slot number, flat, resident, vehicle number, vehicle type, sticker number and remarks. It keeps the allotment in one place for a society or an office.

sections.heading: Keeping the record current
paragraphs: Update the register whenever a vehicle or a resident changes, and note the date in the remarks. The type column helps separate two-wheelers and cars. A visitor parking list can be kept on a separate page. It is a record for your society and not a legal document, so follow your own bylaws.

sections.heading: A list in two columns
paragraphs: The list has item, quantity and a tick box in two columns, so a weekly or monthly shop fits on one page. Type the items first, or print it blank and write by hand.

sections.heading: Shopping with less waste
paragraphs: Check the kitchen before you write the list and group items by where they are in the shop. For a month of shopping, plan the staples once and the fresh items each week. Share the page with the family so everyone adds what they need. It is a list and not a price tracker, so note prices in the margin if you want to compare.

sections.heading: A different maze each time
paragraphs: Choose one of three sizes and make as many different mazes as you want. Each has a start and an end, and an optional answer page shows the way through.

sections.heading: Choosing the right size
paragraphs: Start with the smallest size for young children and move up as they get confident. Every maze can be solved, and the answer page lets a parent or teacher check quickly. Print several for a class or a long journey, and give a pencil. Make a new set whenever you need more.

sections.heading: Cards for a family cookbook
paragraphs: Each card has the dish name, serves, prep and cook time, and space for ingredients and method. Choose a full page, a half page or four to a page.

sections.heading: Writing recipes you will reuse
paragraphs: Write the quantities as you really cook, and note any change you make to the method. Use two layouts for different needs, a large card for a favourite and small cards for quick notes. Collect the cards in a folder or a box, and give a set to someone as a gift. Keep the dish name large so it is easy to find.

sections.heading: Grids from 4 by 4 to 9 by 9
paragraphs: Choose 4 by 4, 6 by 6 or the classic 9 by 9 grid, at three difficulty levels, and print one to four puzzles on a page with an answer page.

sections.heading: Picking a level
paragraphs: Use the small grids for children who are learning the rules and the 9 by 9 grid for adults. Each puzzle is made to have one answer. Start on the easy level, and move up when the puzzles feel quick. Make a fresh set for each lesson or trip, and keep the answer page separate.

sections.heading: Marking an achievement
paragraphs: Type the name and the wording, add the date and pick a border. One landscape page is made for each name, and you can print many in one go.

sections.heading: Making it special
paragraphs: Say what the achievement is, such as finishing a project, winning a contest or reaching a goal. Print on heavy paper, sign with the two lines and hand it over in person. It is a personal certificate from you and not an official document.

sections.heading: Dot grids for kolam and rangoli
paragraphs: The page offers diamond, square, triangle, staggered and hexagon grids, from one to six on a page, so you can practise a design before you draw it on the floor.

sections.heading: Practising and designing
paragraphs: Start with a small grid and join the dots with a pencil to plan the pattern. Try different grids to see how the same idea looks. Children enjoy the dots as a guide, and a larger grid helps for a festival design. Print a few pages so you can keep the best ones.

sections.heading: Tasks, helpers and dates
paragraphs: The checklist has common party tasks, a column for who does them, a date and a done box. It suits birthdays and home parties.

sections.heading: Planning ahead
paragraphs: Start two weeks before and write the guest list and the budget on the page. Give children simple tasks, so they feel part of the party. Plan the food around the number of guests and any dietary needs. Tick each item as you finish, and keep the page where you can see it.

sections.heading: Naps and night sleep on one page
paragraphs: The log has columns for the date, time asleep, time awake, total hours and notes, so you can see a pattern over several days. A week fits on one page.

sections.heading: Using the log
paragraphs: Write the times when you notice them, and add up the total at the end of the day. A log shows patterns and helps you talk to a doctor with real information. It does not say how much sleep a baby needs, because that is different for each child, so ask your paediatrician if you are worried. Keep the pages together.

sections.heading: Letters, numbers or words to trace
paragraphs: Each sheet has grey letters, numbers or words to trace, followed by a blank row to write on, on guide lines for children. You can trace a child's own name.

sections.heading: Helping a child write
paragraphs: Start with large letters and a short session, and praise the effort. The guide lines help with size and spacing, and you can include capital and small letters. Print a new sheet each day, and keep the finished ones to show progress. Use a pencil that is comfortable for small hands.

sections.heading: Wet and soiled, with the time
paragraphs: The log has time, wet and soiled ticks and a notes column, one page for each day. It is a simple record that you can fill in quickly.

sections.heading: Why parents keep a diaper log
paragraphs: A log helps you see patterns and gives a clear record to share with a doctor. It does not say what is normal, because that depends on the baby, so ask your paediatrician about any worry. Use the notes for a change in colour or type. It works for cloth nappies and disposables alike.

sections.heading: Fair teams in seconds
paragraphs: Paste the names, choose how many teams you want or how many people per team, and the tool shuffles them into groups. You can also just shuffle the order, which is handy for deciding who goes first. When the number does not divide evenly, a few teams get one extra person.

sections.heading: Using it in class or at a match
paragraphs: Use it for a class activity, a game in the park, a project group or a quiz night. Because the groups are random, nobody can say the teams were picked unfairly. If you need some people to stay together, make the groups first and move the names by hand. Shuffle again if you want a fresh draw.

sections.heading: Picking without repeats
paragraphs: Paste a list of names and the picker chooses one or more at random. A name that has been picked is not picked again in the same draw, so a group of winners is always different people.

sections.heading: Raffles, turns and giveaways
paragraphs: Use it to choose who answers next in class, who gets a prize in a giveaway or who does the washing up. Keep the list visible so everyone can see it is fair. If two people share a name, add an initial to tell them apart. Run it live on a screen for a raffle so people watch the draw.

sections.heading: Cards from your own words
paragraphs: Type your own words, names or short phrases and the page makes bingo cards in 3 by 3, 4 by 4 or 5 by 5 grids, with an optional free space. Every card is mixed differently, so players do not all win at once.

sections.heading: Planning a bingo game
paragraphs: Make more words than squares so the cards differ, and print one card for each player. Call the words from a separate list, and let players mark with a pen or a counter. It suits parties, classrooms, baby showers and family evenings. Make a themed set for a festival or a topic you are teaching.

sections.heading: Practice sheets and a full chart
paragraphs: Choose the tables you want, up to 20, and print a practice sheet, a shuffled practice or a full multiplication chart. The shuffled version mixes the questions so children do not just memorise the order.

sections.heading: Helping children learn
paragraphs: Start with one table at a time and move on when it feels easy. Use the shuffled sheet for a quick test, and print the chart for a wall or a notebook. Print a fresh mixed sheet each day, and mark it together. Keep sessions short and praise progress.

sections.heading: A sign guests can scan
paragraphs: The sign shows the network name, the password and a QR code that phones scan to join. Guests do not have to type a long password or ask.

sections.heading: Placing and protecting the sign
paragraphs: Put the sign in a living room, a cafe or an office reception. Choose whether to show the password in words, or only as the QR code. A printed password can be read by anyone who sees the sign, so use a guest network and change the password if you need to. Test the QR code with your own phone before you print.

sections.heading: A record of what was decided
paragraphs: The page has meeting, date and place lines, a list of attendees, the agenda, a discussion area and an action table. It gives a clear record of who decided what.

sections.heading: Writing useful minutes
paragraphs: Write the decisions and the actions, not every word that was said. In the action table, write the task, the person and the date. Circulate the minutes soon after the meeting and file a copy. A society committee, a club or a small team can use the same page for each meeting.

sections.heading: Flat by flat, month by month
paragraphs: The register has columns for flat number, resident, month, amount due, paid on, payment mode, receipt number and balance. It gives a single page view of who has paid.

sections.heading: Keeping the register tidy
paragraphs: Fill it in on the day payment is made and write the receipt number so the two records match. Use one page for a month or a block of flats. It is a working record for the committee, not a legal accounts book, so keep your proper accounts as your rules require. Issue a receipt for each payment.

sections.heading: Even grids or one big photo
paragraphs: Join two to nine photos in an even grid, or choose a layout with one big photo and smaller ones. Adjust the spacing, the corners and the background colour, then download a JPG or PNG.

sections.heading: Getting a clean collage
paragraphs: Pick photos with a similar light, so the collage looks balanced, and order them so the story reads from left to right. Use a bit of spacing and rounded corners for a modern look. Download PNG for the best quality or JPG for a smaller file. Your photos stay on your device while you work.

sections.heading: A round seal or a rectangular stamp
paragraphs: Type the text, choose a round or rectangular shape, pick an ink colour and a worn look, and save a PNG with a see-through background. The text curves along a round seal.

sections.heading: Using the stamp image
paragraphs: Place the PNG on a document, a bill or a PDF in your editing app. It is a design for your own use and not an official seal, so do not use it to pretend an authority has approved something. Keep the text short so it stays readable, and try the worn look for a rubber stamp feel.

sections.heading: The pictures inside a PDF
paragraphs: The tool saves every photo and picture stored inside a PDF at its original quality, in one ZIP. There is no page limit and nothing is uploaded.

sections.heading: When it finds nothing
paragraphs: If a PDF has no embedded pictures, or if every page is a scan, there is nothing separate to extract. A scanned page is one big picture, so you get the page and not the objects on it. Drawings and text are not pictures. If you want whole pages as images, use the PDF to images tool instead.

sections.heading: Watching a goal fill up
paragraphs: The tracker has a goal and a target at the top, then rows for the date, amount saved, total so far and notes. It is a plain paper way to see progress.

sections.heading: Staying motivated
paragraphs: Write a goal that you can picture, such as a phone, a trip or an emergency fund, and add each deposit as it happens. It does not decide how much you should save and it does not connect to a bank. Share the page with a friend or family member if you are saving together, and tick off milestones.

sections.heading: Day, place, stay and cost
paragraphs: The itinerary has columns for day, date, place, stay, travel, booking reference and cost. It puts the whole trip on a page.

sections.heading: Planning a smooth trip
paragraphs: Write the bookings as you make them, with the reference number, so you can find them quickly. Print a copy and keep it in your bag as a backup for a dead phone. For a long trip, use more than one page. It does not search for hotels or flights, so use it as the place where your plan comes together.

sections.heading: Service, cost and billing date
paragraphs: The tracker has columns for service, cost, billing date, paid through and cancel by. Seeing every recurring payment on one page helps you decide what to keep.

sections.heading: Cancelling what you do not use
paragraphs: Write the date you must cancel by, so you do not roll into another year. Include gym, school and app fees as well as streaming. Do not write passwords on the page. Review it every few months and cross out what you stopped using, and add the monthly total to see the real cost.

sections.heading: A row for each month
paragraphs: The tracker has a row for each month and columns for electricity, water, gas, internet, mobile and total. You can see bills side by side across the year.

sections.heading: Noticing changes
paragraphs: Write each amount when the bill arrives and add the total at the end of the row. A sudden jump in one column is a prompt to check for a leak or a fault. You can change the column names for a shop or an office. Keep the bills themselves for as long as you need them.

sections.heading: Puzzles from your own words
paragraphs: Type a list of words and the page hides them in a grid. Choose easy to hard directions, from four grid sizes, and print an answer page for checking.

sections.heading: Using it for learning
paragraphs: Make a puzzle for spelling practice, vocabulary, a festival or a class topic. Start with easy directions for younger children, and use the harder levels for older ones. Keep the word list short for a small grid. Print one for each child and keep the answer page for the teacher.

sections.heading: Sets, reps and weight
paragraphs: The log has columns for date, exercise, sets, reps, weight and notes. It suits the gym and home exercise.

sections.heading: Making progress visible
paragraphs: Write the weight and reps as you finish each set, so next time you know what to beat. Use the notes for how it felt. It does not plan your workouts. It works for strength training and can be adapted for running or yoga with the notes column. If you have a health condition, ask a doctor before you begin a new routine.

sections.heading: A box for every day
paragraphs: The tracker has a row for each habit and a box for every day of the month, with a days column to count what you completed.

sections.heading: Building a habit that sticks
paragraphs: Start with two or three habits and make them small enough to do on a bad day. Fill in the box the same day, and do not worry about a missed one. Seeing a row of ticks is the reward. Print a fresh sheet for each month and keep the old ones to see how far you have come.

sections.heading: Two columns and a tick box
paragraphs: The list has two columns of items with a tick box for each, so it fits a trip, a holiday or a hostel move on one page.

sections.heading: Packing without forgetting
paragraphs: Write the list a few days early and add things as you think of them. Pack by groups, such as clothes, papers and chargers. For a family, print one list for each person. Keep the page for next time so you can start from it.

sections.heading: Every service on one page
paragraphs: The log has columns for date, odometer, work done, workshop, cost and next service due. It builds a service history you can show later.

sections.heading: Keeping a useful record
paragraphs: Write the entry the day of the service and staple the bill to the page. Use a separate page for each vehicle. A good record helps you remember when the next service is due and is useful when you sell the vehicle. Follow the service schedule in your owner's manual.

sections.heading: Where the money goes
paragraphs: The tracker has columns for date, item, category, amount and payment mode. It is for personal or family spending.

sections.heading: Using categories well
paragraphs: Use a few simple categories such as food, travel, bills and fun, so the totals mean something. Add up each category at the end of the month. It is a record and not a budget, so use it with a budget sheet if you want a plan. Keep the pages private because they show how you spend.

sections.heading: Recording small payments
paragraphs: Each voucher has a number, date, paid to, purpose, amount, an approver and a receiver. Four vouchers fit on a page.

sections.heading: Using vouchers properly
paragraphs: Write the voucher when the cash leaves, get the signatures and attach the bill. A voucher records the payment and does not replace the bill. Add your business name at the top, and keep the used vouchers together. Number them in order so none go missing.

sections.heading: A draw on one phone
paragraphs: Add the names, run the draw and pass the phone around. Each person taps their own name to see who they got, and then hides the screen for the next person.

sections.heading: Keeping the secret
paragraphs: The organiser should not look at the results. Set any rules, such as keeping couples apart, before the draw, and note that some rules can make a draw impossible. Nothing is sent to anyone, so you can use it in the room. Agree on a budget and a date for the gift exchange.

sections.heading: Orders, advances and balances
paragraphs: The register has columns for date, customer, phone, item, amount, advance, balance and delivery date. It suits tailors, bakers, makers and small shops.

sections.heading: Staying on top of orders
paragraphs: Write each order when it is taken and note the advance received. Work out the balance and tick off the delivery. It is a register and not a bill, so give your customer a proper receipt. Keep customer phone numbers private and store the pages safely.

sections.heading: Teaching children about money
paragraphs: The log has columns for date, money received, what it was spent on, amount spent and balance. Children can see where their money goes.

sections.heading: Using it at home
paragraphs: Let the child write the entries and check them together once a week. It builds the habit of saving and noticing. How much pocket money to give is a family decision. The same page works with cash, a bank account or a digital wallet, as long as you write the balance.

sections.heading: Who came, when and why
paragraphs: The register has columns for date, name, phone, whom to meet, purpose, in time, out time and signature. It suits offices, shops and societies.

sections.heading: Keeping it useful
paragraphs: Put it at the entrance and ask each visitor to fill a line. The phone number helps you reach someone later. Keep the register in one safe place and decide how long you keep old pages. Check your own rules to see if a record is required for your premises.

sections.heading: Names, ideas and budgets
paragraphs: The list has columns for name, relation, gift idea, budget, bought and given. It helps you plan gifts for festivals and occasions.

sections.heading: Planning early
paragraphs: Write the list a month ahead so you can buy without a rush. Set a budget for each person and add up the total. Tick bought and given so you do not forget or repeat. Keep the old lists to remember what you gave last year, and to avoid giving the same thing twice.

sections.heading: One picture, many posts
paragraphs: Choose a grid of 1 to 5 by 1 to 5 and the tool cuts your picture into numbered pieces, in square or portrait shape, and gives them in a ZIP.

sections.heading: Posting the pieces in order
paragraphs: Post the pieces in the order of the numbers so the full picture forms on your profile. Pick a high quality picture so the pieces stay sharp. Keep the original for yourself. On a phone, open the ZIP in your files app to get to the images.
